Kurschak Tile

AreaGeometryTriangles
Game: This picture has a star inside a square, and there is nothing to win: its triangles can be moved to cover three quarters of the square.
How to play: Press Move them to watch nine triangles slide into three corners. Tick names or hint for labels and guide lines, press Reset to start over, or drag the step handle and use arrow keys to look at one step at a time.

Red triangles are thin, blue triangles have three equal sides. The step handle at the bottom runs from 0 to 30.

Look for the math

A twelve-pointed star looks nothing like a neat area answer, yet its triangles can be moved to fill three quarters of the square around it. That is the whole trick behind Kürschak's theorem.

The claim, exactly

The page says: the area of a regular dodecagon inscribed in a unit circle is 3. The logic test checked that claim from the drawn coordinates, not by quoting it: cutting a circle of radius 1 into twelve equal wedges gives 12 × (1/2) × sin(30°) = 6 × 1/2 = 3. The square around that circle has side 2 and area 4, so the dodecagon is 3/4 of it. The test also checked the scaling law 3R² for radii from 0.01 to 250.

Why the same pieces fit twice

The dodecagon is cut into 24 thin isosceles triangles with angles 15°, 15°, 150° and 12 equilateral triangles. Both families share the side R/(2 cos 15°): the identity 2 sin 15° = 1/(2 cos 15°) makes a dodecagon edge exactly as long. So two thin triangles meeting at their long bases make a rhombus whose other sides match the blue triangles. Tick Show hint to see how the pieces pair up around the centre.

Three quarters of the square

Outside the dodecagon, each corner of the square takes two thin triangles and one equilateral one: 8 thin and 4 regular triangles in all. Their total area is R², leaving 4R² - R² = 3R² for the dodecagon. The test checked that all 36 pieces are the advertised shapes, that the 12 outside triangles cover exactly the difference, and that the nine pieces moved by the applet land on three complete corners; the fourth corner is left outlined so you can see the pattern.

A very old bound on pi

With R = 1 the circle's area is π and the inside shape has area 3, so the page finishes with π > 3. That is true: an inscribed shape is smaller than its circle. The original applet animates the move in 30 steps and offers only Show names, Show hint, Reset and Move them; the step handle here is an addition so you can inspect every frame. The original leaves one moving thin triangle 15° off its stored corner while it travels, then draws it at the stored position when it arrives; the port keeps that stored final position.

Try ticking Show names and pressing Move them: the letters A to O show how the square's corners and the star's tips line up, and the last step leaves one corner empty for you to fill in your head.
